title: Identifiable Equivariant Networks are Layerwise Equivariant
claim: A symmetry acting on the input propagates through the network as latent symmetries on each layer until it reaches the output.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right, pink arrows marking group action at input, latent layer, and output
description: A single left-to-right diagram of a neural network used for image segmentation. On the left is a tilted photo of a green lizard on a rock, with a pink circular arrow labeled G that shows a rotation of the input. Next come two stylized fully connected layers drawn as grey nodes and lines. In the middle are three isolated nodes with pink curved arrows between them, which depict neuron permutations in the latent space. Dots indicate omitted layers. Two more grey layers follow, then a tilted black-and-white segmentation mask of the lizard on the right. A black horizontal arrow labeled G runs across the top from input to output. The pink arrows draw the eye first, because they carry the idea that the group action propagates.
caption: An image segmentation model is equivariant to rotations of the image. Our main result implies that the group action on the input propagates through the network via latent symmetries (e.g., neuron permutations), until it reaches the output.
abstract: We investigate the relation between end-to-end equivariance and layerwise equivariance in deep neural networks. We prove the following: For a network whose end-to-end function is equivariant with respect to group actions on the input and output spaces, there is a parameter choice yielding the same end-to-end function such that its layers are equivariant with respect to some group actions on the latent spaces. Our result assumes that the parameters of the model are identifiable in an appropriate sense. This identifiability property has been established in the literature for a large class of networks, to which our results apply immediately, while it is conjectural for others. The theory we develop is grounded in an abstract formalism, and is therefore architecture-agnostic. Overall, our results provide a mathematical explanation for the emergence of equivariant structures in the weights of neural networks during training -- a phenomenon that is consistently observed in practice.
